trickyParts: The Tailscale Service is registered with pulumi.Parent(comp) alone, never with newDispatchKubernetes's `child` options: those carry the Kubernetes provider and a DependsOn on the GKE cluster, neither of which belongs on a tailnet resource.

The Service's Protect follows deletionProtection rather than being hard-coded true: a resource a remote component protects on its own is one the consumer cannot unprotect, so a deliberate teardown would need an edit of the component.

The single-generation rendering of DISPATCH_SIGNING_KEY is the bare RandomPassword result with no Sprintf or join, so a running deployment's Secret data is byte-identical and this release's first apply plans no change to it. TestDispatchDefaultSigningKeySetIsTodaysOneKey pins the whole input map of that one RandomPassword (Length 64, Special false, no keepers) as well as the rendering.

databaseWaitsFor's value reaches no resource: the seed refusal's ApplyT keeps the input's own dependencies, and dependsOnInput reads only those, so chaining the two both refuses a seed and carries the ordering.

Round 2's migration step told a consumer to run `pulumi state delete` on its own tailscale.Service. The reviewer showed it is refused for exactly the stacks that need it: a stack that passed the Service's Name as tailnetService has the component depending on it, since the SDK puts the input's dependency in the Construct request's Dependencies and that becomes the component's own DependsOn, and `pulumi state delete` refuses a resource something in state depends on; `--target-dependents` would remove the Dispatch component and every child of it from state. Round 3 replaces that step with retainOnDelete in two applies and says why the state edit is not the route.

openQuestions: No live pulumi preview of the consuming stack can run here: no pulumi CLI, no GCP credential, and the consumer does not pin this release yet. The mocks prove the declaration and prove nothing about what the live stack would plan.

Whether svc:dispatch already exists in the target tailnet is unverifiable in this pod, which holds no Tailscale credential. It is not a failure if it does: the Tailscale provider's create is an upsert (VIPServices().CreateOrUpdate), so the component adopts the live Service and overwrites its comment, ports and tags. What matters for the cutover is the order of the two declarations, which the README's new section 'Moving a stack that declares the Service itself' states: the consumer takes its own tailscale.Service out of its state without deleting the Service (pulumi state delete) before the apply that moves the pin, because removing the declaration with the Service still in that state deletes the Service the component has just adopted.
discoveredComplexity: Measured, and the reading INFRA-561's design needs: a consumer's pulumi.DependsOn on the component does NOT reach the component's children. Constructed with an upstream URN in ConstructRequest.Dependencies, the engine recorded the Cloud SQL instance's dependencies as exactly its own two siblings, the Network example-dispatch-network and the Connection example-dispatch-services, and nothing of the consumer's. pulumitest.Construct was extended to pass that field, and TestConstructComponentDependsOnDoesNotReachTheChildren records it. So databaseWaitsFor is the only way to order that child after a consumer's resource, and the explicit input is not redundant with a component-level DependsOn.

The simplify pass (ce-simplify-code, three reviewers at head ffcf361f) applied six findings: the test binary is built once per rotation row rather than once per process start, which cut TestAStagedKeyRotationAcrossThreeAppliesKeepsPeopleSignedIn from 36.9 s to 9.0 s; svc:<name> got one spelling (tailnetServiceName), since removing the apply-time refusal left three independent copies of the prefix; the duplicated listener assertion, a redundant m.Named lookup and an unrolled schema assertion were folded back into the tables that already held them. Three findings were recorded and skipped: hoisting dependsOnInput into a shared internal package (it would edit aws/, outside this change, and D7 decided the per-package copy); the staged-rotation constants' two single-key aliases (they name the rotation's four settings, which is the test's subject); and sharing one process start/replace helper with TestTwoProcessesAnnounceTheirBuildOnce (outside this diff).

Round 2, the reviewer's findings: the component does not fail on a Service that already exists under its name — the Tailscale provider's create is an upsert, so it adopts the live Service and overwrites its comment, ports and tags. The hazard is the consumer's own declaration, which, removed while the Service is still in that stack's state, deletes the Service the component has just adopted. The README gains a migration section and the changelog fragment a sentence for it. Also corrected: 'the consumer cannot unprotect a component's child' (pulumi state unprotect can; what is absent is a resource option that reaches the child), and the grant text, which said a grant on the front door's tags does not reach the Service — it does, since the component gives the Service those same tags.

Round 3: a child's own Protect overrides the one it would inherit from its component, so the earlier reason for tying the Service's Protect to deletionProtection — 'no resource option of the consumer's program reaches a component's child' — was wrong twice over: a resource transform on the component does reach each child (README 'Providers and transformations'), and the SDK takes the parent's Protect only when the child names none (pulumi/sdk/v3 v3.268.0, go/pulumi/context.go:1450-1453). The true reason is that a fixed Protect on this child could then be changed only by such a transform or by a state edit.
